analysis.answer: Current law makes possession of any amount of cannabis a misdemeanor punishable by up to 90 days in jail. The text changes this by allowing adults 21 and older to possess up to one ounce of cannabis and making it no longer an offense.
The text likely reduces direct justice-system costs by eliminating arrests, court cases, and potential jail time for possessing small amounts of cannabis.
Adults 21 and older who use cannabis benefit by avoiding criminal penalties and records. Law enforcement, courts, and local jails benefit from a reduced administrative and custodial burden.

With the threat of criminal penalties removed, the number of adults who possess and consume cannabis may increase. Law enforcement agencies will redirect the resources previously spent policing small-scale possession toward other activities.

The text addresses the legal and systemic burdens caused by criminalizing minor cannabis possession. The mechanism directly resolves this by legalizing possession of up to one ounce for adults 21 and older and eliminating the associated offense.
Adults 21 and older gain the legal discretion to possess small amounts of cannabis without facing criminal charges.

The broader impacts of decriminalizing cannabis are disputed. Some researchers find it decreases justice system costs and arrests without substantially increasing crime or heavy drug use, while others find it is associated with increases in youth access, substance abuse, and impaired driving.
Because the text simply removes an offense and does not create a new regulatory program, there is little to no loss in administration.
This is a statutory change that can be amended or repealed by the legislature under ordinary procedures.
